A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Single Index Bandits work. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite extensive renumbering and relocation.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic simulations, sparse linear experiments, runtime measurements, and evaluations on Forest Cover Type and Yahoo News.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds GSTOR simulation results, a DR Lasso comparison, and a sparse nonlinear experiment.

M1.justification: The Stein estimator, regularization, STOR, ESTOR, and GSTOR procedures remain unchanged. Algorithms 1–3 retain the same steps; the added explanations and sparsity discussion do not replace their procedures.

E1.justification: v2 adds a sparse high-dimensional scenario with the nonlinear square reward function, whereas v1 evaluates only linear rewards in that setting. The four low-dimensional scenarios and both real-world datasets remain.

E2.justification: Figure 2 and Appendix L add DR Lasso Bandit to the sparse comparisons, alongside the retained LinUCB and LinTS baselines. The existing low-dimensional and real-data baseline sets remain unchanged.

E3.justification: The new sparse nonlinear experiment deliberately fits LinUCB, LinTS, and DR Lasso with linear reward models, introducing an additional misspecification protocol. Settings for retained experiments, including horizons, dimensions, arm counts, and tuning multipliers, remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The added sparse square-function experiment tests robustness to nonlinear rewards when baselines assume linearity. v2 also compares GSTOR against misspecified GLB methods in the existing synthetic scenarios; v1's original misspecification tests remain.

E5.justification: Both versions report averages over 20 simulation repetitions and 10 independent real-data runs. v2 adds no confidence intervals, error bars, significance tests, seed disclosures, or changed repeated-run counts.

E6.justification: v2 adds GSTOR synthetic regrets and runtimes, DR Lasso results, and sparse nonlinear regret curves. For example, Table 2 reports GSTOR regrets of 1397.26 and 519.18 for square and fifth-power rewards. Figure 1 and the real-data results, moved from Table 2 to Table 3, are retained.

T1.justification: v2 corrects multiplicative mu factors to inverse-mu factors in regret derivations and explains this dependence in Remark D.2. It also exposes C in ESTOR's bound, replaces Lemma 7.5's proof with an algebraic proof in Lemma E.1, and states STOR's sparsity-independent exploration tradeoff. Headline regret rates remain unchanged.

C1.justification: The introduction drops v1's explicit claim to the first SIM estimator attaining optimal error under the stated minimal assumptions. The central contributions—single index bandits, the three algorithms, sparsity extensions, and their headline regret rates—remain.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly identifies fixed i.i.d. contexts as a limitation and states that the fitted covariate distributions used in real-data experiments lack theoretical guarantees. It adds explanations of GSTOR's exploration overhead and potential benefits, but overstates its superiority under misspecification: Table 2 shows lower regret than GLM-TSL, not UCB-GLM.

D1.justification: The reproducibility disclosures retain the same Apple M3 hardware, hyperparameter rules, tuning procedure, synthetic data generation, and real-data preprocessing. No code release, data-access change, or additional implementation specification is supplied; added runtimes are experimental results.

R1.justification: Appendix A substantially expands the former related-work section. It discusses closely related nonlinear ridge bandits, concurrent single-index modeling for batched bandits, additional monotone SIM estimators, and a detailed comparison with FALCON+. These additions materially develop the paper's novelty positioning and distinctions from existing approaches.

P1.justification: Related Work moves from Section 2 to an expanded Appendix A, a new Appendix B summarizes technical novelty, and the main text gains proof sketches and explanatory passages. The introduction and limitations are revised, and the numbered appendix hierarchy becomes Appendices A–L.

P2.justification: Figure 2 expands from one panel to two and includes DR Lasso; a new Table 2 tabulates synthetic regrets. The real-data table is renumbered, and the document adopts ICLR headers and typography. Figure 1 is unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 strengthens empirical support with a relevant sparse baseline and nonlinear robustness test, corrects regret derivations, and improves discussion of prior work and applicability limits. These are useful, bounded gains. The new blanket claim that GSTOR outperforms misspecified GLB methods is contradicted by its UCB-GLM comparisons in Table 2, tempering the improvement without outweighing the added evidence and transparency.
